title: Design Front Middle Back Queue
description: Design a queue with O(1) push/pop at the front, middle, and back, using two balanced deques with a shared rebalance step.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Design a queue supporting pushFront(val), pushMiddle(val), pushBack(val), popFront(), popMiddle(), popBack() (each pop returning -1 if the queue is empty). When there are two possible middle positions (an even-length queue), pushMiddle inserts closer to the front, and popMiddle removes the one closer to the front.

blocks.caption: Two balanced deques keep the boundary between them exactly at the true middle.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["pushFront / pushBack","Insert at the front / rear of the queue"],["pushMiddle","Insert at the middle; for even length, closer to the front"],["popFront / popBack","Remove and return the front / rear, or -1 if empty"],["popMiddle","Remove and return the middle; for even length, the one closer to the front"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

Needing O(1) access to the front, back, AND middle simultaneously is solved by splitting the sequence into TWO deques, a left half and a right half, with the boundary between them always sitting at the true middle. Front and back operations touch the outer ends of left and right respectively, while middle operations touch the inner boundary, exactly where the two deques meet.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: The "two balanced halves" idea is the same one behind a median-tracking two-heap structure, just using deques (for O(1) end access) instead of heaps (for O(1) extremum access).
3. Understand the Problem

Picture two balanced stacks of cards side by side, like a seesaw kept level: the left pile never has more than one extra card compared to the right pile. Because they stay balanced this way, the boundary between the two piles IS always the middle of the combined sequence, so operating at that boundary is just as fast as operating at either outer end.

blocks.caption: Two balanced halves make the middle just as cheap to reach as either end.

items: Maintain the invariant: left.size() equals right.size(), or left.size() is exactly one more than right.size().
pushFront/pushBack simply push to the appropriate outer end, then rebalance if the invariant broke.

pushMiddle/popMiddle touch the inner boundary: if left is currently larger, the operation happens on left's back; otherwise on right's front, which correctly implements the "ties favor the front" rule.

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
pushFront(1), pushBack(2), pushMiddle(3), pushMiddle(4), then popFront(), popMiddle(), popMiddle(), popBack(), popFront().

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: The results [1, 3, 4, 2, -1] exactly match the official LeetCode example. The second popMiddle() call, on the tied-size state left=[4], right=[2], correctly returns 4 (from the left side), demonstrating the "ties favor the front" rule.
5. How Should We Think?

A single array or list supports all six operations, but pushFront/popFront and pushMiddle/popMiddle require shifting O(n) elements, since inserting or removing anywhere except the very end of a plain array-backed list is linear.

Splitting into two balanced deques turns every operation into O(1): front/back operations are plain deque end operations, and middle operations become an end operation on whichever half is currently allowed to shrink (the larger one, or left in a tie), followed by a cheap rebalancing step that moves at most one element between the two deques.
6. Brute Force Solution
Use a single list, inserting and removing at the exact computed index for each operation, relying on the underlying structure to shift elements as needed.
7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["pushBack / popBack","O(1) amortized","Insertion/removal at the very end of a dynamic array"],["pushFront / pushMiddle / popFront / popMiddle","O(n)","Shifting all elements after the insertion/removal point"],["Space","O(n)","The single backing list"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: Front and middle operations both require shifting a large fraction of the elements on every call, which is unacceptable for a queue meant to support frequent middle access.
8. Optimize the Solution

Split the queue into two deques, left and right, maintaining left.size() in {right.size(), right.size() + 1}. Front/back operations touch the appropriate outer end directly. Middle operations touch the boundary: pushMiddle moves one element from left to right first if left is currently strictly larger (making room), then pushes to left's back; popMiddle removes from left's back if left.size() >= right.size(), otherwise from right's front. A shared rebalance step, called after every operation, restores the invariant by moving at most one element between the deques.

items: Front ops: left.addFirst / left/right.pollFirst. Back ops: right.addLast / right/left.pollLast.
Middle ops: operate on left's back when left is the larger (or tied) half, otherwise on right's front, then rebalance.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Splitting a sequence into two balanced halves gives O(1) access at three points (both outer ends plus the boundary) instead of just the ends.
A shared rebalance step, run after every mutating operation, keeps the size invariant intact with at most one element moved per call.
The "left is allowed one extra element" convention is what makes the front-favoring tie-break for middle operations fall out naturally, without any special-case code.

blocks.text: 12. Final Summary

Design Front Middle Back Queue is solved with two balanced deques, left and right, kept within one element of each other in size. Front and back operations touch the outer ends directly, while middle operations touch the shared boundary, giving O(1) time for all six operations, with a lightweight rebalance step preserving the size invariant after every call.
